cells.tense: You are steering by a light you have already picked out.
cells.ask: Tell one person today which direction you keep coming back to. Say it as something you're doing, not weighing. Then go a week without asking anyone to confirm it.
cells.core:
Direction isn't a decision you make once and defend. It's a light you keep your face turned toward, and most days you do it without announcing it. You have one. You know which way you're pointed, and it shows in small choices that don't need justifying to anybody. That steadiness is quiet enough that the people around you may not notice it.

What holds it up is support, and the calm kind — someone standing behind the direction you picked, not pushing you toward it. Let that in without turning it into a debt. Keep it by handing the same steadiness to one other person who is still choosing, and let them pick differently from you.
cells.sheetLine: You keep your face turned toward a light you already chose.
cells.verb: choosing which light to move toward
cells.place: the pull toward what you actually want, felt before it's named

cells.tense: You are standing in a future where the direction has to already be proven right.
cells.ask: For one week, before each decision, say out loud which way you're pointed right now. Name it, then make the call. If you can't name it, make the same call once and stop.
cells.core:
You want the direction settled before you move. Every option gets weighed, every possibility tested for whether it will hold, and the weighing has quietly become the whole relationship with it. Nothing gets chosen, because nothing clears the bar you've set for choosing. Meanwhile you're defending a certainty that hasn't arrived.

What's needed is smaller. Knowing one thing from another is enough — real enough to land without an argument. Pick one aim for a day and let the others wait. The test isn't whether it proves right. It's whether you can tell what you're moving toward while you're still moving, and let what you notice sharpen the aim instead of freezing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're defending a certainty you haven't let arrive.
cells.verb: choosing which light to move toward
cells.place: the pull toward what you actually want, felt before it's named

cells.tense: You had a direction and you closed the door on it at some point.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you stopped doing that you can still describe with warmth. Do it once, badly, this week. Tell no one for three days.
cells.core:
There was a light you were following and something shifted. Now when people ask what you're aiming at, the honest answer is you don't know, and you say it like it's permanent. The pull toward something hasn't disappeared. It's just been still for a while and you've stopped expecting it to move.

What draws it back isn't willpower. It's a small piece of care — the kind that doesn't tire you out because the impulse isn't forced. Start with what you can't help doing anyway, the thing that was already yours before you lost the thread. Do it once. The direction re-registers on its own; you don't have to assemble it from scratch.
cells.sheetLine: The pull hasn't gone. It stopped, and you let it.

cells.tense: You are already steering, and you talk about it like the situation steering you.
cells.ask: Say 'this is mine' about a thing you've been calling the situation. Once, out loud to yourself counts. Then do the next small thing as the person who chose it.
cells.core:
Look at the last month. The turns you took, what you kept, what you let go — they run in one line, and the line isn't random. You have a direction. You don't call it yours; you call it what the work required, or what the timing made obvious. The steering is happening. Only the claim is missing.

Naming it isn't meant to change the direction. It's meant to put the pen back in your hand, because a choice you don't claim gets spent on whatever's loudest. Support here is simple: one thing you've been calling necessity, done as a choice. Make the next small decision as the one who made it, and you can keep the direction instead of following it.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering already. You call it the situation.

cells.place: the pull toward what you actually want, felt before it's named

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person has chosen a star and knows what it is — the record supports only a capacity for direction, not that any particular direction is already felt. Reader's likely objection: 'I don't have a clear direction, that's exactly my problem' — the Balanced cell could then land as flattery. The ask survives being wrong: naming the direction they keep returning to is the same act whether they have one or not, and the Too Little cell carries the no-direction case with the exit in the partner's act. Sentence that serves the writer more than the person: any version of 'you already know which star is yours' — cut it, replaced with what they actually asked for.
